description-meta: "A research program on measuring learning in human–AI activity: capturing process data, coding it with validated LLM classifiers, modelling interdependence with network methods, and representing it so people can act on it."
---

People have always worked with tools, and those tools have always changed. What
has not changed is the need to say something about a person on the basis of
evidence they did not produce alone.

My program approaches that problem through the chain of inference implied by
**evidence-centered design** — observing activity, recording it as data, coding
and modelling that data, and warranting claims about learning. Theory guides each
link: what I observe, what I record and code, how I model, and what claims are
worth making. Below, each section is a link in that chain and the work that
contributes to it.

::: {.panel}
**The core commitment.** What we want to measure is learning. What we must
account for is *interdependence* — the structure that arises as people and tools
respond to and build on one another's contributions. Interdependence is not the
measurand; it is what has to be accounted for so that evidence of joint activity
can license claims about individuals.
:::

## Observing interaction: the Trace platform

::: {.strand}
[01 — Observe]{.strand-label}

Accounting for interdependence requires a reliable way to capture interaction in
the first place. *Trace* is a learning analytics platform that records the
actions and interactions of human writers and GenAI tools during writing
activity. It exists in two versions.

The **web platform** is typical of learning analytics work: students read sources
in a PDF viewer, write in a text editor, and talk to a GenAI tool in a contained
chat window. It logs source views, keystrokes, prompts and responses, and
copy/paste events. It has supported a single-session study with roughly 250
students in a large master's research methods class, and a six-week longitudinal
study with a cohort of master's students in law. It is currently in use by a
research team I am not part of, studying how students respond to feedback on
writing they are permitted to produce with AI.

Capturing the same activity without an instrument of this kind means screen
recording and hand-coding video — across hundreds of sessions, or dozens of hours
per participant.

The **browser extension**, built on outputs from my DARPA-funded knowledge
management work and funded by the ARC, widens the horizon of observation to more
authentic activity. It collects the same data, but distributes collection across
the tools learners already use — Google Docs, Overleaf, GenAI chat interfaces —
rather than tools specified by researchers. It is in closed beta in preparation
for in-the-wild studies.
:::

## Coding interaction: LLM-based classifiers

::: {.strand}
[02 — Code]{.strand-label}

Data on its own is not understanding. We need ways to identify and interpret the
relevant pieces of it. The coding schemes I develop combine top-down,
theory-driven work with bottom-up, data-driven work.

An example of why that combination matters: my colleagues and I are building a
multimodal scheme for categorising interactions between students and GenAI during
writing, drawing on cognitive and sociocultural theories of writing and on
emerging work on AI literacy. Both literatures warrant a code for *verifying
sources*. Across the sessions we have analysed, that code has almost no
instances — and it stays in the scheme. A scheme induced from the data alone
would never have shown that the behaviour was missing.

Coding with LLMs introduces a validity problem earlier methods do not face.
Classifications are stochastic, sensitive to prompt design, and indexed to a
particular generation of models, so agreement established once does not stay
established. My current work extends codebook-to-classifier approaches with
additional validation: structured refinement of code definitions, hold-out
testing against human coding, and stability testing across repeated
classification. The aim is classifiers whose outputs can be checked, so the
claims built on them are warranted rather than assumed.
:::

## Modelling interdependence: networks and simulation

::: {.strand}
[03 — Model]{.strand-label}

Relationships among codes are explored through models. Traditional approaches
either isolate individual actions or treat the system as an undifferentiated
whole. The argument I made in my dissertation — that interdependence among coded
actions reveals differences aggregate accounts cannot — has organised my work
since, and has held in settings I could not have anticipated at the time,
including human–AI interaction.

**Epistemic network analysis** (ENA) and **ordered network analysis** (ONA) have
been my principal instruments for that argument. I am a co-author of
[`rENA`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=rENA) and
[`ncodeR`](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ncodeR), and of the mathematical
foundations of the method. Recent extensions combine these models with social
network analysis and **graph neural networks**, so that social and cognitive
interdependence can be modelled together. Much of the technical capability
already existed; what it lacked was a framing that treated these structures as
interdependence. GNNs can represent them, but the dimensions they yield are hard
to interpret — ENA's visualisations give a way of reading those dimensions in
terms of relationships among actors and codes, so gains in representational power
do not cost the ability to say what the model found.

Models of interdependence are new enough that we know little about how they
behave. I approach this through **method-facing simulation**: generating coded
traces with known structure, then evaluating what analytic pipelines recover from
them. With colleagues and students I extended a stochastic generator of coded
discourse to vary the degree of sequential ordering, and compared what ENA and
ONA recover across that range. The two diverge at low levels of ordering.
Disagreement between them is therefore *diagnostic* — it sends the researcher
back to the data with a specific question about ordering, and removes the option
of not asking it.
:::

## Making claims: writing with generative AI

::: {.strand}
[04 — Claim]{.strand-label}

With appropriate data, coding schemes, and models, my students, colleagues and I
have begun to make specific claims about writing with GenAI. Taken together, the
work suggests that writing with GenAI is in itself neither good nor bad — what
matters is *how* people write with it.

In a study led by my doctoral student, we compared the questions university
writers asked a GenAI tool with those they asked a human tutor while revising a
multi-source essay. Writers working with GenAI asked more questions in shorter
exchanges, and asked them pragmatically — direct questions about conceptual and
procedural knowledge, rather than the indirect requests for feedback that
characterised the tutor condition.

The effect of condition on revised essay quality was **mediated by the structure
of that questioning**. With the interdependence among question types in the
model, access to the tool no longer explained performance. A frequency-based
composite over the same codes detected no such mediation. What distinguished
stronger revisions was not that writers used GenAI, but how they questioned it —
a difference the revised essays themselves could not reveal.

Related work uses the same models to distinguish knowledge telling from knowledge
transformation during AI-assisted writing, and to separate genres by interaction
structure alone.
:::

## Representing activity: Trace Replay

::: {.strand}
[05 — Represent]{.strand-label}

Making claims from process data requires a link most assessment work leaves
implicit. Data, codes and models are not evidence anyone can act on until they
are represented in a form a person can read. That was tenable when a reader could
reconstruct the activity behind the evidence themselves. With human–AI
interaction, they cannot.

Through co-design with learners and educators, I have developed *Trace: Replay*,
which represents GenAI-assisted writing at three levels:

- **Micro** — replays interaction data in semantically and theoretically
  meaningful segments.
- **Meso** — renders those segments as process-level representations using
  simplified network models.
- **Macro** — aggregates across a session, for instance the distribution of
  activity between writer and tool.

The levels are designed to be traversed, so a macro pattern can be interrogated
at the meso level and checked against the record at the micro level. The next
study asks whether learners can use these representations to assemble evidence of
their own process, and whether educators reading it arrive at claims they can
defend.
:::

## Where this is going

**Scale.** Studying how people write with AI across disciplines, institutions and
levels of study. The methodological problems become unavoidable at scale:
classifiers validated on one corpus have to hold across heterogeneous settings,
and models of interdependence have to behave consistently across contexts the
original studies never varied.

**Domain.** GenAI is being taken up across activities that resemble writing in
structure if not in content — most immediately data analysis and research writing
in graduate education. Extending the chain there tests its generality. I expect
capture and modelling to transfer and coding schemes to need rebuilding, but
which parts travel is exactly what the work would establish.

**Agentic systems.** Working with an agent differs from working with a chatbot.
Human–AI interactions change in kind, number and timing, and AI-to-tool and
AI-to-AI interactions become targets of study for the first time. Each link in
the chain has to be reconsidered — what is worth capturing, which codes apply,
and what interdependence means when most of the actors are not people.

**Consent at the edge of capture.** Once collection extends onto tools people
chose for their own purposes, consent cannot be a single act at the start of a
study; it is distributed across time and tools and has to be renegotiated as the
activity moves. Assessment sharpens this, because the standard privacy remedy is
unavailable — anonymisation defeats the purpose of an assessment, which exists
precisely to attribute evidence to a person. I plan to approach it as I
approached representation: through co-design with the people whose activity is at
stake.
